items.title: 61521_David Albert Francis oral history interview
items.q: one outstanding, and that's my boy, Binks "Dizzy" Gillespie; he calls me David

ctx.x: But I had this job lined up with Roy Eldridge, and so I joined his band, like, the first week in

July, and that's when my name was changed from David to Panama. That's the reason when I meet someone that calls me David right now, it's someone that knew me before 1939. You know, you can always tell the people who knew me before 1939, because they would call me David, with the exception of a few musicians, one outstanding, and that's my boy, Binks "Dizzy" Gillespie; he calls me David, and he never called me Panama.

items.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: he’d have both jaws out like this you know, like Dizzy Gillespie.

ctx.x: Do different musicians that play different ways ‘cause you to react certain ways as a drummer?

Well yes. I am very competitive. In fact when I worked with Roy Eldridge, he was of the same mentality. And we used to go out and look for jam sessions and look for guys to cut you know. Because back then it was just like sports. I mean music was like sports. You and I can be the best of friends. And you play drums, I play drums. But when we got on the bandstand it was a different ball game. Everything went out the window. I mean I’m competing with you and you are competing with me. And that’s why, you know,…
You know tell us about your concept of what the drummer does in the ensemble. What role does the drummer bring to jazz music?
